Surely in this are signs for those of ˹sound˺ knowledge.”* (30:22). Language and colour are named because both are inherited without choice, both vary endlessly, and neither has any bearing on a person's worth. A single chapter elsewhere pairs the same observation with the creation of spouses and the compassion placed between them (30:21 — *“And He has placed between you compassion and mercy.”*). The argument from diversity is that a species this internally varied, yet unified in structure, is not the product of accident. Accident does not produce variety within a pattern; it produces noise.

**The Lowliness of the Body Is Also a Sign**

A third reading, recorded by al-Ghazzālī among others, takes "in your selves" as a reference to the body's undignified processes — the fact that food and drink pass through it and leave it as waste. The purpose of the observation is not disgust but the demolition of pride. A man who remembers what his body is cannot sustain the self-importance that blocks reflection. The Qur'an makes the same move by describing human origins in material terms: *“Let people then consider what they were created from! ˹They were˺ created from a spurting fluid, stemming from between the backbone and the ribcage. Surely He is fully capable of bringing them back ˹to life˺”* (86:5–8). The last clause states the argument outright: the one who assembled this from such a beginning has no difficulty reassembling it.

The Qur'an issues this command directly elsewhere, and the phrasing is close to a rebuke: *“Have they not reflected upon their own being? Allah only created the heavens and the earth and everything in between for a purpose and an appointed term. Yet most people are truly in denial of the meeting with their Lord!”* (30:8).
verses.22:
> In heaven is your sustenance and whatever you are promised

**A Report That Fixes the Quantity**

The practical consequence of a fixed supply is stated in the tradition with unusual directness. Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh reports the Prophet ﷺ as saying: "O people, fear Allah and be moderate in seeking a living, for no soul will die until it has received all its provision, even if it is slow in coming. So fear Allah and be moderate in seeking provision; take that which is permissible and leave that which is forbidden." (Sunan Ibn Mājah 2144, graded ṣaḥīḥ by Dārussalām). The report contains both halves of the doctrine: the provision is complete and cannot be missed, and because it cannot be missed, the pursuit of it must not become immoderate or unlawful. That is exactly the instruction implied by verse 22. A supply already located in heaven does not need to be seized by any means available on earth.

**The Guarantee Is Stated for Every Living Thing**

The Qur'an generalises the point beyond human beings: *“There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah. And He knows where it lives and where it is laid to rest. All is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record.”* (11:6). Three features are named — the guarantee, the knowledge of each creature's dwelling, and the written record — and all three reappear in verse 22's claim that provision is in heaven. Another passage describes the mechanism of surplus and restriction: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘Surely ˹it is˺ my Lord ˹Who˺ gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills of His servants. And whatever you spend in charity, He will compensate ˹you˺ for it. For He is the Best Provider.’”* (34:39). The compensation clause matters here, since it answers the fear that giving reduces what is left.

**The Promise Is Stored in the Same Place**

The second half of the verse puts "whatever you are promised" alongside provision, in the same location. The commentators read the phrase as everything God has apportioned for each person, which includes the resurrection and the judgment sworn to at the chapter's start (51:5–6 — *“Indeed, what you are promised is true And the Judgment will certainly come to pass”*). Placing the two together does important work. A man anxious about next month's food and a man doubting the Day of Judgment are, on this verse, making the same category error: assuming that what he cannot see does not exist or has not been arranged. Provision arrives from a place he cannot enter; the promised day will arrive from a place he cannot inspect. Both are fixed, both are recorded, and both are outside his control. The verse treats the second doubt as no more reasonable than the first.

Verses 17 to 19 described people who gave away a recognised share of their wealth. Verse 22 answers the unspoken objection to that practice. Giving looks like loss when supply is thought to originate in the purse; it does not look like loss when supply originates in heaven. The Qur'an makes the same point in the language of a loan: *“And donate from what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you, and you cry, ‘My Lord! If only You delayed me for a short while, I would give in charity and be one of the righteous.’”* (63:10). The provision is described as given by God before it is described as spent by the owner, which is the same ordering as verse 22. The man who gives from a supply located in heaven is not reducing his store; he is drawing on it in the direction it was meant to flow.
verses.23:
> Then by the Lord of heaven and earth! ˹All˺ this is certainly as true as ˹the fact that˺ you can speak

**Lord of Heaven and Earth Names Everything Just Cited**

The two titles are not generic. The heaven has just been named as the location of provision and promise (51:22 — *“In heaven is your sustenance and whatever you are promised”*); the earth as the field of signs (51:20 — *“There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith”*); and the self, which belongs to the earth's material, as the second field (51:21 — *“as there are within yourselves. Can you not see”*). Swearing by the Lord of heaven and earth is swearing by the owner of the entire evidential base the chapter has assembled.

The same pairing appears in the oath series that opens another chapter (37:5 — *“˹He is˺ the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, and the Lord of all points of sunrise”*), and in the description of God as the one who gives authority over whom He wills (59:6 — *“But Allah gives authority to His messengers over whoever He wills.”*). A title that covers both domains is the only title adequate to guarantee a claim about both, since the promise concerns bodies made of earth and an outcome administered from heaven.

**Why Speech and Not Sight**

Verse 21 ended with a challenge to see, and this verse shifts to speaking. The shift is deliberate. Sight can fail — distance, darkness, a defective eye, an object hidden. Speech cannot be doubted by the one performing it, because there is no gap between the act and the awareness of the act. The verse selects the faculty with the shortest distance between experience and certainty, which is why the comparison works as a standard rather than as a metaphor. It also quietly answers the mockers of verse 12, who had been talking. Their question "when is this day" was itself an act of speech, performed with total confidence in its own occurrence. The verse takes that confidence and turns it into the measure of what they refuse.

**The First Argument Block Closes Here**

Verses 1 to 23 form a complete unit: oaths by the created order, the sworn statement that the promise is true and the judgment will fall, a diagnosis of the mockers, the description of the reverent and their three practices, signs on the earth and in the self, provision in heaven, and now an oath by the Lord of both. The unit moves from nature to conduct to nature again to God Himself. What follows changes register completely — the chapter turns to narrative, beginning with the honoured guests of Abraham (51:24 — *“Has the story of Abraham’s honoured guests reached you ˹O Prophet˺”*). The turn is not a departure from argument but a change of evidence: after signs that can be observed, the chapter produces history that can be checked, in the same land, along the same trade routes. The oath of verse 23 is the hinge between the two.
verses.24:
> Has the story of Abraham’s honoured guests reached you ˹O Prophet˺

**"Has It Reached You?" Is a Recognised Opening**

The formula *hal atāka ḥadīth* appears at the head of several passages and always introduces a report the hearer is about to be given in full: *“Has the story of Moses reached you ˹O Prophet˺?”* (79:15), *“Has the news of the Overwhelming Event reached you ˹O Prophet˺?”* (88:1), *“Has the story of the ˹destroyed˺ forces reached you ˹O Prophet˺—”* (85:17), and the same question about Moses at 20:9 — *“Has the story of Moses reached you ˹O Prophet˺”*. The interrogative is not a real question. It signals that what follows is a communication, and it puts the hearer in the position of a recipient rather than a judge. Some commentators note the verse can equally be read as a statement: you have heard tell of Abraham's honoured guests. Either way the effect is to place the story inside a known tradition before any detail is given.

**Who the Honoured Guests Were**

The commentators record the guests as angels in human form, with estimates of three, ten, or twelve, and one of them identified as Gabriel. The parallel accounts are consistent with this: *“And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺.”* (11:69), and *“They reassured ˹him˺, ‘Do not be afraid! We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.’”* (11:70). Nothing in the narrative announces them as angels at the outset, which is why Abraham's reaction develops as it does — a greeting, a meal, then fear when the meal is not touched. The concealment is the point of the story's structure. Had they arrived visibly as angels, there would have been no hospitality, no suspicion, and no lesson in either.

**Honoured by Two Parties**

*Mukramūn*, honoured, can be read in two directions at once, and both are supported. They are honoured by Abraham, who gives them the best greeting and the best food he owns without knowing who they are. They are also honoured by God, being chosen messengers on an errand of both mercy and judgment. The same word elsewhere describes the honoured servants who do not speak until God has spoken (21:26–27 — *“who do not speak until He has spoken, ˹only˺ acting at His command”*), which fixes the rank of the guests from the divine side.

**Hospitality Is Tied to Belief in the Tradition**

The practice displayed here is not presented in the Qur'an as a cultural courtesy of ancient Arabia alone; the tradition attaches it to faith itself. Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet ﷺ as saying: "Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not harm his neighbor. Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should entertain his guest generously, and anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet." (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6018). The three items are joined to the same condition of belief, and hospitality sits between neighbourliness and speech. Abraham's conduct in the following verses is the narrative form of that instruction, which is one reason the chapter selects this episode at all.

**The Same Story Told Elsewhere With Different Emphasis**

This account is close to the versions in Hūd and al-Ḥijr, and other aspects of Abraham's story appear in 14:35–41 — *“˹Remember˺ when Abraham prayed, “My Lord! Make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure, and keep me and my children away from the worship of idols”* and 37:83–109 — *“And indeed, one of those who followed his way was Abraham”*. The variations are purposeful rather than inconsistent. In Hūd the wife's laughter is mentioned and Abraham's pleading for Lot's people follows the news (11:71 — *“And his wife was standing by, so she laughed, then We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob”*, 11:74 — *“Then after the fear had left Abraham, and the good news had reached him, he began to plead with Us for the people of Lot”*); in al-Ḥijr the emphasis falls on Abraham's astonishment at his own old age (15:54 — *“He wondered, “Do you give me good news despite my old age? What unlikely news!””*); in aṣ-Ṣāffāt the glad tidings are given directly by God (37:112 — *“We ˹later˺ gave him good news of Isaac—a prophet, and one of the righteous”*). Here in adh-Dhāriyāt the emphasis is on the honour shown to the guests and on the mission they carry. Each version selects what its chapter needs, and this chapter needs a story about a promise received by a man who served his guests first.
verses.25:
> ˹Remember˺ when they entered his presence and greeted ˹him with˺, “Peace!” He replied, “Peace ˹be upon you˺!” ˹Then he said to himself,˺ “˹These are˺ an unfamiliar people.”

**Two Greetings in Two Grammatical Cases**

The exchange is recorded with a detail that only Arabic preserves. The angels' greeting arrives in the accusative, which reads as "we wish you peace" — a salutation directed at another. Abraham's reply comes in the nominative, "peace be upon you," a statement about peace itself. The commentators point out that the second form is fuller and firmer than the first. The Qur'an legislates precisely this movement: *“And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things.”* (4:86). Abraham's answer is the better greeting, returned to visitors he has not identified and has no reason to flatter. The scene therefore opens with a small act of moral precision that sets the character of everything that follows.

**The Greeting Given Is the Greeting of Paradise**

The words exchanged here are not a local custom that happens to appear in scripture. They are the currency of the destination the chapter has been describing. The people of the gardens are greeted with the same word: *“Those who believe and do good will be admitted into Gardens, under which rivers flow—to stay there forever by the Will of their Lord—where they will be greeted with ‘Peace!’”* (14:23). Speech in that place is described as consisting of nothing but good and virtuous words (56:26 — *“only good and virtuous speech”*). The believers are greeted with it in this world too: *“When the believers in Our revelations come to you, say, ‘Peace be upon you!’”* (6:54). Abraham's house in this scene is behaving like the Garden, which is why the episode can carry religious weight rather than being a mere anecdote about manners.

**"An Unfamiliar People" Names a Real Problem**

The phrase *qawm munkarūn* means people not recognised, unknown. The word belongs to the same root that produces *munkar*, the wrong or improper thing, and its basic sense here is simply "not known to me." the commentators differ on whether Abraham said this aloud to his guests or to himself and to his household. The self-addressed reading is supported by what happens next, since he turns away quietly to his family rather than confronting the visitors (51:26 — *“Then he slipped off to his family and brought a fat ˹roasted˺ calf”*). The other reading makes the remark a polite inquiry into their identity. Both are coherent with the narrative, and the ambiguity may be intentional: the verse records an observation about strangers whose identity is genuinely unknown, and leaves its addressee where the story leaves it.

**Strangers Are the Ordinary Form of Angels**

The concealment is consistent with how angels appear throughout the Qur'an. They come to Abraham as messenger-angels bearing good news and are not recognised at first (11:69 — *“And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺.”*); they come to Lot in a form that puts him in anguish because he cannot protect guests he believes to be men; they come to Mary in human shape (19:17 — *“screening herself off from them. Then We sent to her Our angel, ˹Gabriel,˺ appearing before her as a man, perfectly formed”*). A visible angel would end the story before it began, since no host could behave naturally in front of one.

**The Greeting Is Legislated for Every House**

The exchange recorded here does not remain a story. The Qur'an turns the same practice into law for believers: *“O believers! Do not enter any house other than your own until you have asked for permission and greeted its occupants. This is best for you, so perhaps you will be mindful.”* (24:27). Permission and greeting are joined, and both precede entry. A second verse carries the rule into ordinary social life: *“However, when you enter houses, greet one another with a greeting ˹of peace˺ from Allah, blessed and good.”* (24:61). The greeting exchanged in Abraham's tent is therefore the ground of a standing etiquette, and the description attached to it in that verse — blessed and good — matches the speech of the Garden, which consists of nothing but good and virtuous words (56:26 — *“only good and virtuous speech”*). A scene about unknown visitors becomes the basis of a rule governing every door a believer enters.
verses.26:
> Then he slipped off to his family and brought a fat ˹roasted˺ calf

**Rāgha Means He Went Quietly**

The verb translated as slipped off is *rāgha*, from a root carrying the sense of turning aside, departing stealthily, moving without drawing attention. It is not the ordinary word for going. The choice describes a host who leaves his guests without announcing that he is leaving to feed them. The etiquette is exact: a guest told "I am going to slaughter something for you" is placed under an obligation and may protest, while a guest whose host quietly disappears is simply presented with food. The commentators note the parallel formulation elsewhere, where Abraham hastens to bring a roasted calf (11:69 — *“Then it was not long before he brought ˹them˺ a ˹fat,˺ roasted calf”*), and both features — speed and silence — belong to the same practice. The verse records not merely what was given but how the giving was managed.

**He Did Not Ask Who They Were First**

The verse's placement after the remark about unfamiliar people is significant. Having noted that these are unknown visitors, Abraham's next recorded act is feeding them. He does not interrogate them, does not require a purpose for the visit, and does not condition the meal on an explanation. The order is a rule in itself: identify the need, then satisfy it, and ask questions afterwards if questions remain. Abraham's later question about their mission comes only after the meal is placed before them (51:31 — *“˹Later,˺ Abraham asked, “What is your mission, O messengers?””*).

**The Quiet Departure Protects Everyone**

Going to his family rather than issuing an order in front of the guests has a second effect. The household is not put on display, and the guests are not made aware of the cost being incurred on their behalf. Hospitality that announces its own expense converts the guest into a debtor. The verb *rāgha* covers both sides of that discretion: he leaves without ceremony, and the arrangement is made without the visitors hearing it arranged. The Qur'an's praise of Abraham elsewhere summarises the character displayed here: *“Truly, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning ˹to his Lord˺.”* (11:75). Forbearance and tenderness are exactly what the quiet departure shows.

**The Guest Holds a Claim, Not a Hope**

Hospitality in the tradition is an obligation attached to belief rather than a kindness left to mood. Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet ﷺ binding three behaviours to one condition: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should entertain his guest generously, should not harm his neighbour, and should say what is good or keep silent (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6018). The adverb carries the weight — generously, not adequately. Abraham's conduct matches it exactly: a fattened calf, prepared at once, for visitors he cannot identify and who have claimed nothing. The same report ties hospitality to belief in the Last Day, which places it inside this chapter's subject. A household that expects a reckoning feeds strangers before asking who they are, because the feeding is part of the account being kept. Nothing in the verse suggests a receipt was issued to the guests, and that absence is the practice in its pure form.
verses.27:
> and placed it before them, asking, “Will you not eat?”

**"Will You Not Eat?" Is an Invitation, Not an Instruction**

The question form is deliberate Arabic courtesy. A host who says "eat" issues a command and puts the guest under pressure; a host who says "will you not eat?" offers and leaves the answer open. The negative interrogative carries a further shade of urgency — it expresses the host's hope that the guest will eat, without demanding it. The verse therefore records both the generosity and the restraint of the same man in one clause. He has spent a fattened calf and does not intend to extract gratitude for it. The phrasing is the linguistic form of the discretion already shown by the quiet departure: the guest's freedom is preserved even at the moment of greatest investment by the host.

**The Question Also Functions as Alarm**

Read in sequence with what follows, the same words carry a second edge. The guests have entered unannounced, accepted the greeting of peace, and now sit before untouched food. A host's polite question in that situation is also a probe. The Qur'an's parallel account makes the resulting unease explicit: *“And when he saw that their hands did not reach for the food, he became suspicious and fearful of them.”* (11:70). The suspicion is generated by the untouched plate, not by anything the visitors said.

**Nothing Is Asked in Return**

Abraham's question seeks no payment, no news, no service, and no introduction. The hospitality of the two preceding verses is unconditional in the strict sense: it is extended before the guests' identity, purpose, or ability to reciprocate is known. The Qur'an elsewhere frames prophetic service in the same terms, with the messenger asking no wage from his people. The narrative here makes the point concretely, through food rather than doctrine. A man who feeds strangers and then asks only "will you not eat?" has set the standard against which the later request for information — what is your mission? (51:31 — *“˹Later,˺ Abraham asked, “What is your mission, O messengers?””*) — can be seen as secondary. He gave first, and he asked afterwards.

**The Same Formula Is Used Against the Idols**

One other place in the Qur'an contains this exact question, and the contrast could not be sharper. Standing before the images his people set out with food, Abraham turns to them and says: *“Will you not eat ˹your offerings˺? What is wrong with you that you cannot speak?”* (37:91–92), and then strikes them with his right hand (37:93 — *“Then he swiftly turned on them, striking ˹them˺ with his right hand”*). Addressed to idols, the polite interrogative is irony: a meal is placed before them and nothing happens, because nothing is there. Addressed to guests in his own tent, the same words are sincerity. The two uses of one formula measure the distance between a living visitor and a dead image. In this scene the refusal to eat falls nearer the second case than Abraham can yet know, and the fear described in the next verse is the alarm of a man who has found that his guests do not behave like men.

> ˹They did not eat,˺ so he grew fearful of them. They reassured ˹him˺, “Do not be afraid,” and gave him good news of a knowledgeable son

**"Do Not Be Afraid" Is the Standard Angelic Opening**

The reassurance is a formula the Qur'an uses whenever angels appear to people who cannot yet identify them. In Hūd it arrives with the reason attached: *“They reassured ˹him˺, ‘Do not be afraid! We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.’”* (11:70). In al-Ḥijr it is joined immediately to the good news: *“They reassured ˹him˺, ‘Do not be afraid! Surely we give you good news of a knowledgeable son.’”* (15:53). The repetition across chapters shows the pattern: fear, removal of fear, then the message. The order is not arbitrary. A terrified recipient cannot receive news, so the news waits until the fear has been addressed. Verse 28 in this chapter compresses the same sequence into a single sentence.

**The Good News Names Knowledge, Not Strength**

The son promised is *ghulām ʿalīm*, a boy who will be knowing. The quality selected is intellectual and spiritual rather than physical or political. Nothing is said about his strength, his wealth, his descendants, or his rank, and the adjective is the same one used in the parallel account (15:53 — *“They reassured ˹him˺, “Do not be afraid! Surely we give you good news of a knowledgeable son.””*). Elsewhere the promise to Abraham is described with a different quality: *“So We gave him good news of a forbearing son.”* (37:101), where forbearance — *ḥilm*, the capacity to hold one's temper under provocation — is named. The two descriptions belong to the two sons in the traditional reading and together give the character of the promised lineage. In this verse the emphasis falls on knowledge, which fits a chapter whose argument has just moved through signs, certainty, and reflection.

**Which Son Is Promised**

The majority of commentators identify the knowledgeable son here as Isaac, and the identification is well supported. The parallel in Hūd names him explicitly and adds a grandson: *“And his wife was standing by, so she laughed, then We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob.”* (11:71). A later chapter confirms the sequence by giving Isaac as a distinct, subsequent glad tiding: *“We ˹later˺ gave him good news of Isaac—a prophet, and one of the righteous.”* (37:112). A minority reading takes the son here as Ishmael, which requires the promise to be a separate announcement. The stronger position is Isaac, since the scene is continuous with the accounts in Hūd and al-Ḥijr that name him, and the wife's reaction in the next verse belongs to Sarah.

**God Gives the News Through Intermediaries**

Verse 28 says the angels gave him good news, while aṣ-Ṣāffāt says God gave it: *“We ˹later˺ gave him good news of Isaac—a prophet, and one of the righteous.”* (37:112). The commentators reconcile the two by noting that God gave the tidings through the angels as His messengers. Both statements are therefore true at different levels, and the pattern is consistent with the chapter's fourth oath, which swears by the angels administering affairs by command (51:4 — *“and ˹the angels˺ administering affairs by ˹Allah’s˺ command”*). Here is the administration at work on a single household: a decree from above delivered by couriers below. The same mechanism operates in the announcement to Mary, delivered by a messenger in human form (19:19–21 — *“He replied, “So will it be! Your Lord says, ‘It is easy for Me. And so will We make him a sign for humanity and a mercy from Us.’ It is a matter ˹already˺ decreed.””*).

**The News Is Impossible, and the Verse Says So Only by Implication**

Nothing in verse 28 mentions the obstacle. The reader learns it in the following verse, from Sarah's own mouth: a barren, old woman (51:29 — *“Then his wife came forward with a cry, clasping her forehead ˹in astonishment˺, exclaiming, “˹A baby from˺ a barren, old woman!””*). The narrative arrangement is effective because it lets the promise be stated in its full, unqualified form before the impossibility is raised. The good news arrives as good news, not as a problem to be negotiated. When the objection comes, it comes from the human side and is answered by a statement about God's decree rather than by a biological explanation (51:30 — *“They replied, “Such has your Lord decreed. He is truly the All-Wise, All-Knowing.””*).

The same order appears in the announcement to Mary and in the sending of Moses to Pharaoh, where the instruction is to speak gently so that the hearer may become mindful or fearful in the right way (20:44 — *“Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful ˹of My punishment˺.””*).

> Then his wife came forward with a cry, clasping her forehead ˹in astonishment˺, exclaiming, “˹A baby from˺ a barren, old woman!”

**She Was Standing By**

The parallel account in Hūd places her in the room and records a different first reaction: *“And his wife was standing by, so she laughed, then We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob.”* (11:71). The commentators discuss the laughter, some reading it as relief after the fear, others as the astonishment of a woman whose body had returned to fertility, others simply as joy. The two accounts are not in conflict so much as in sequence: a woman present at an extraordinary announcement reacts with a sound and a gesture, then with words. Adh-Dhāriyāt records the physical reaction; Hūd records the laughter and the naming of the son and grandson. Between them the scene is complete.

**Her Husband Is Included in the Impossibility**

The fuller version of her objection names both parties: *“She wondered, ‘Oh, my! How can I have a child in this old age, and my husband here is an old man? This is truly an astonishing thing!’”* (11:72). The addition matters, because it moves the case from a personal anomaly to a joint one. Two people beyond the age of childbearing cannot produce a child by any ordinary route, and the verse in Hūd makes her say so.

**The Ages Traditionally Given**

The commentators record Abraham at about one hundred and twenty years old at this point, and Sarah at about ninety-nine. Those figures come from transmitted accounts rather than from the Qur'anic text, and their value here is not precision but proportion: the promise concerns two people at the extreme end of a long life, one of them barren throughout it. The Qur'an itself makes the age explicit in another version, where Abraham responds to the news with his own astonishment: *“He wondered, ‘Do you give me good news despite my old age? What unlikely news!’”* (15:54). The point of the ages is that the birth cannot be explained by any natural recovery of fertility. It is a creation, not a cure.

**Astonishment Is Not Disbelief**

The angels' answer in the parallel account shows how the reaction is judged: *“They responded, ‘Are you astonished by Allah’s decree? May Allah’s mercy and blessings be upon you, O people of this house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, All-Glorious.’”* (11:73). The question is a rebuke, but it is a gentle one, and it is immediately followed by a blessing on the household. Nothing in either account suggests Sarah is charged with unbelief. Astonishment at an impossible announcement is the natural response of a person who takes the world seriously; denial would be a refusal to take the announcer seriously. The distinction is the reason this scene can appear in a chapter about certainty without damaging its subject.

**The Same Reaction at Mary**

A later announcement produces the same shape of response. Mary asks: *“How can I have a son when no man has ever touched me, nor am I unchaste?”* (19:20). Her objection, like Sarah's, is built completely from facts about her own situation, and it includes a defence of her character. The answer is identical in structure: *“He replied, ‘So will it be! Your Lord says, ‘It is easy for Me. And so will We make him a sign for humanity and a mercy from Us.’ It is a matter ˹already˺ decreed.’”* (19:21). Two women, two impossible births, two objections made of evidence, and the same reply in both cases. The pairing is one reason this narrative block sits in a chapter whose subject is the certainty of a promise that has not yet arrived.
verses.30:
> They replied, “Such has your Lord decreed. He is truly the All-Wise, All-Knowing.”

**The Same Answer Given to Mary**

The parallel is close enough to be treated as a fixed form. When Mary raises her objection, the reply runs: *“Your Lord says, ‘It is easy for Me. And so will We make him a sign for humanity and a mercy from Us.’ It is a matter ˹already˺ decreed.”* (19:21). Three elements recur — ease for God, a purpose in the form of a sign and a mercy, and a matter already settled. The adh-Dhāriyāt version compresses all three into one clause plus two names.

**"How" Is Answered With "Who"**

Sarah's objection was a question about process, and the answer is a statement about agency. This is a general feature of the Qur'an's handling of the resurrection, which is the chapter's main subject. When asked how dead bones will be restored, the reply points to the one who made them first and knows every creation (36:78–79 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being”*). When the reviving of land is offered as an analogy, the emphasis falls on the one who sends the wind and drives the cloud (35:9 — *“And it is Allah Who sends the winds, which then stir up ˹vapour, forming˺ clouds, and then We drive them to a lifeless land, giving life to the earth after its death. Similar is the Resurrection”*). The method is never supplied because the method is not the difficulty. The difficulty is always whether the agent is capable, and the answer to that is a description of the agent rather than of the process. Verse 30 is that answer in its shortest form.

**A Rebuke Delivered as a Blessing**

The parallel account adds the tone of the reply: *“Are you astonished by Allah’s decree? May Allah’s mercy and blessings be upon you, O people of this house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, All-Glorious.”* (11:73). The question is corrective and the greeting that follows it is warm. The household is addressed collectively and blessed, which tells the reader that the astonishment has not damaged the standing of the house. This is how the Qur'an corrects a believer's surprise: it names the surprise as misplaced, then confirms the relationship. In adh-Dhāriyāt the correction is compressed into the two divine names, which do the same work by implication — a person who knows and orders wisely is not to be measured against a household's expectations.

**The Story Now Turns to Its Second Errand**

With the announcement settled, the narrative returns to the reason the visitors came. Abraham's next question is about their mission (51:31 — *“˹Later,˺ Abraham asked, “What is your mission, O messengers?””*), and the answer concerns a people marked for destruction. The shift is abrupt and it is characteristic of these accounts: a household receives a promise of life at the same moment as a region receives a decree of death, and both decrees are delivered by the same messengers in the same visit. The chapter holds the two together because its argument requires both. A God who gives a son to a barren woman and destroys a city of transgressors is administering one order, and the administration is the same one sworn by in the fourth oath of the chapter's opening (51:4 — *“and ˹the angels˺ administering affairs by ˹Allah’s˺ command”*).

The chapter's subject is resurrection, and this scene supplies its most intimate evidence. The objection to resurrection is always the same: decayed material cannot be reassembled. The Qur'an answers it by pointing at origins: *“And they argue with Us— forgetting they were created—saying, ‘Who will give life to decayed bones?’ Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time, for He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of every created being.’”* (36:78–79). The story of Abraham's household is that answer acted out. A womb closed for a lifetime is opened by decree, and the mechanism is no more explained than the mechanism of resurrection will be. The same logic runs through the account of human beginnings elsewhere: *“We did create you from dust, then from a sperm-drop”* (22:5), and *“No female ever conceives or delivers without His knowledge.”* (35:11).

> ˹Later,˺ Abraham asked, “What is your mission, O messengers?”

**He Now Calls Them Messengers**

The address *ayyuhā al-mursalūn* — O messengers — shows that the disguise has ended. At the start of the scene they were an unfamiliar people (51:25 — *“˹Then he said to himself,˺ “˹These are˺ an unfamiliar people.””*); after the reassurance and the promise they are recognised by their function. The title is not a guess. Angels who announce a birth that cannot occur naturally, and who speak with the authority of "so has your Lord decreed" (51:30), have identified themselves enough. Abraham's question therefore proceeds from knowledge rather than curiosity, and the respect in the vocative marks the rank he now assigns them. The same title appears in the parallel account in al-Ḥijr (15:57 — *“He ˹then˺ added, “What is your mission, O messenger-angels?””*), where the question is worded almost identically.

**What He Did With the Answer**

The parallel account records the consequence of the reply, and it is the reason this question matters: *“Then after the fear had left Abraham, and the good news had reached him, he began to plead with Us for the people of Lot.”* (11:74). The verse supplies both conditions — fear gone, news received — before describing the pleading, which confirms the significance of the order noted above. Only a man at peace and in possession of a mercy of his own argues for the salvation of others. The pleading is presented as an act of the same character the Qur'an praises in him elsewhere: forbearing, tender-hearted, ever turning to his Lord (11:75 — *“Truly, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning ˹to his Lord˺”*).

**Pleading Against a Decree Already Issued**

Abraham's intercession runs into a limit, and the limit is stated without softening: *“˹The angels said,˺ ‘O Abraham! Plead no more! Your Lord’s decree has already come, and they will certainly be afflicted with a punishment that cannot be averted!’”* (11:76). The exchange shows two things at once. Compassion for people under a decree of destruction is legitimate and is exercised by the Qur'an's greatest exemplar of tenderness. And a decree that has come cannot be argued back. The sequence is not a failure of Abraham's pleading but its correct end: he pleads until he is told the matter is closed, and then he stops. The chapter needs both halves, since its subject is the certainty of decrees.

**The Question Is a Model for Receiving the Unseen**

Abraham does not panic at the presence of angels, does not demand a sign, and does not speculate about their purpose. He asks. The question is short, direct, and respectful, and it is put after the household's own affairs have been settled. The chapter has spent twenty verses arguing that signs require a receiver with certainty (51:20 — *“There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith”*), and it now shows one.

**Asking About an Announced Mission Is Not Prying**

The Qur'an draws a line around inquiry, and Abraham's question sits on the permitted side of it. Believers are told: *“O believers! Do not ask about any matter which, if made clear to you, may disturb you. But if you inquire about what is being revealed in the Quran, it will be made clear to you.”* (5:101). The forbidden question is the one that fishes in hidden matters and then cannot bear the answer. Abraham's is different in kind. His visitors have already identified themselves as messengers and have already delivered one part of their errand to his own household. Asking what remains is not curiosity about the unseen; it is completing a communication the other party opened. The verse models a discipline that believers need: ask about what has been raised, and do not manufacture questions about what has not.
verses.32:
> They replied, “We have actually been sent to a wicked people

**The People Are Not Named in This Version**

Adh-Dhāriyāt leaves the target unidentified at this point. The parallel accounts name them immediately: *“We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.”* (11:70). The omission here is a feature of the chapter's compression. Verses 32 to 34 describe the mission in general terms — a wicked people, stones of clay, marked for the transgressors — and the identification arrives only indirectly, through the evacuation of the believers and the single house of submitters found in the city (51:35–36 — *“Then ˹before the torment˺ We evacuated the believers from the city”*). A reader who knows the story supplies Lot at once; a reader who does not receives a description of a punishment whose logic is stated before its location. Either way the argument is unaffected, since the point is the pattern rather than the place.

**Sent, Not Acting on Their Own**

The reply begins with *innā mursalūn* — we have been sent. The same subordination is stated doctrinally elsewhere: the angels are honoured servants who do not speak until God has spoken and act only at His command (21:26–27 — *“who do not speak until He has spoken, ˹only˺ acting at His command”*). The chapter has already sworn by this fact in its opening verses, where the fourth oath names the angels administering affairs by command (51:4 — *“and ˹the angels˺ administering affairs by ˹Allah’s˺ command”*). Verse 32 is that oath in operation: couriers describing their delivery.

**The Same Vocabulary Describes Pharaoh**

The chapter's next narrative block uses closely related terms for its target. Pharaoh is described as having transgressed all bounds (79:17 — *“˹commanding,˺ “Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺”*), and the mission against him is a seizure rather than a stoning. Elsewhere he is named as a tyrant and a transgressor (44:31 — *“of Pharaoh. He was truly a tyrant, a transgressor”*). The vocabulary of guilt runs through all four accounts that follow in this chapter — Lot's people, Pharaoh, ʿĀd, Thamūd — and in each case the guilt is established before the punishment and is described in moral rather than legal terms. The repetition is the chapter's method: four cases, one pattern, warning refused and consequence executed. Verse 32 states the pattern in its opening clause.

**Two Conditions Could Have Stopped the Punishment**

The Qur'an states the circumstances under which a community is spared, and neither applied here. *“But Allah would never punish them while you ˹O Prophet˺ were in their midst. Nor would He ever punish them if they prayed for forgiveness.”* (8:33). The presence of a messenger and the practice of seeking forgiveness are the two shields, and the people described in verse 32 had rejected the first and abandoned the second. Their messenger had called them to fear and identified himself as trustworthy (26:161–162 — *“I am truly a trustworthy messenger to you”*), and the reply was that he was bewitched (26:153 — *“They replied, “You are simply bewitched”*). The general rule is stated without exception: punishment follows a warning that was refused (17:15 — *“And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺”*). Verse 32 therefore opens the mission statement with a people who have already exhausted the two possibilities that could have kept the stones in the sky.

The Qur'an uses the term as a standing contrast with belief: *“Is the one who is a believer equal ˹before Allah˺ to the one who is rebellious? They are not equal!”* (32:18).

Stones of clay, marked by the Lord for the transgressors (51:33–34 — *“marked by your Lord for the transgressors.””*).
verses.33:
> to send upon them stones of ˹baked˺ clay

**Sijjīl Is Clay That Has Been Fired**

The word used for the stones is *sijjīl*, and it means clay baked hard — material that begins as mud and ends as something with the density and edge of ceramic. The commentators take it as stones of hardened clay. The same word appears in the other accounts of this destruction: *“When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay”* (11:82). *“And We turned the cities ˹of Sodom and Gomorrah˺ upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.”* (15:74). The material is deliberately ordinary. It is not iron, not fire from the sky, not a meteor of exotic composition. It is earth, altered by heat, and the alteration is the only thing supernatural about it.

**The Cities Are Turned Over Before the Stones Fall**

The order in the parallel account matters. The command comes, the settlements are inverted — their uppermost made their lowermost — and then the stones rain down on what is left. The two operations are distinct and sequential. Verse 33 in this chapter mentions only the stones, because its purpose is to describe the mission the messengers were sent on rather than the whole catastrophe. The fuller sequence appears in Hūd and in al-Ḥijr, and another chapter compresses it into a single image: *“We unleashed upon them a storm of stones. As for ˹the believers of˺ Lot’s family, We delivered them before dawn”* (54:34). Read together, the accounts describe a total reversal of a settled landscape followed by a bombardment of its remains.

**A Rain From Above, Where the Roof Was Thought Safe**

The verb used for the stones is one of raining or sending down. The Qur'an notes elsewhere that the people of the Stone Valley carved homes in mountains and felt secure, and were overtaken by a blast in the morning (15:82–83 — *“They carved their homes in the mountains, feeling secure”*) — a different people, but the same structure of false confidence. Verse 33 belongs to that pattern: the instrument of destruction comes from where no defence has been built.

**The Same Word Appears in the Chapter of the Elephant**

*Sijjīl* occurs one other place in the Qur'an, and the context is instructive. Describing the birds sent against the army that came to destroy the Kaʿbah, the text says they pelted them with stones of baked clay (105:4 — *“that pelted them with stones of baked clay”*). Two events separated by centuries use the identical material. In both cases a small, unimpressive projectile destroys an army or a city that considered itself invulnerable, and in both cases the destruction is total.

**Delivered Before Dawn, With the Believers Already Gone**

The timing is specified in another account: the storm of stones came after the believers had been delivered before dawn (54:34 — *“We unleashed upon them a storm of stones. As for ˹the believers of˺ Lot’s family, We delivered them before dawn”*). The instruction to Lot's household was to travel in the dark of night, and their appointed hour was the morning (11:81 — *“Their appointed time is the morning. Is the morning not near?””*). The punishment and the rescue are coordinated to the minute, and the coordination is the reason verse 33's mission statement can be read as justice rather than catastrophe. Stones fall on a city that has already been emptied of everyone who was not part of the crime. What remains is not a mixed population caught in a disaster but a targeted execution carried out on a cleared site.

> marked by your Lord for the transgressors.”

**Precision Excludes Collateral Damage**

A punishment delivered by marked stones cannot strike the wrong person. This is not a small detail in a scene where the guilty city has just been emptied of its believers (51:35 — *“Then ˹before the torment˺ We evacuated the believers from the city”*). The marking guarantees that the evacuation and the bombardment are two halves of one operation rather than a rescue followed by an indiscriminate disaster. The Qur'an insists on this feature of divine punishment repeatedly: no soul burdened with sin bears the burden of another (17:15 — *“No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another.”*), and the record of the day is itemised to the weight of an atom (99:7–8 — *“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it”*). Verse 34 places the same principle inside a historical event. Stones addressed to individuals are the physical form of a reckoning that is personal rather than collective in its execution.

**"By Your Lord" Turns to the Man Hearing It**

The parallel verse makes the address explicit: *“marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers!”* (11:83). The marking is attributed to the Lord of the listener, not of the ancient city, and the second sentence extends the warning across the centuries. The stones are not far from the wrongdoers now being addressed.

**Musrifūn Names the Specific Crime: Excess**

The people the stones are marked for are *musrifūn*, from a root meaning to exceed a limit, to spend or act beyond measure. The word covers extravagance in wealth and in appetite, and it is used of moral excess generally. Its application here is precise: the charge against Lot's people in the Qur'an is not a single act but a settled practice that overstepped what the messenger had set before them. The same vocabulary describes Pharaoh as a tyrant and a transgressor (44:31 — *“of Pharaoh. He was truly a tyrant, a transgressor”*), and the command to go to him is justified by the fact that he has transgressed all bounds (79:17 — *“˹commanding,˺ “Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺”*). Excess is the chapter's word for the state that precedes destruction, in every case it narrates.

**Marking Implies a Prior Register**

Stones do not acquire names by themselves. The marking assumes a list, and the Qur'an speaks of such lists constantly: everything written in a perfect record (11:6 — *“All is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record”*), the two recording angels noting every word (50:17–18 — *“As the two recording-angels—˹one˺ sitting to the right, and ˹the other to˺ the left—note ˹everything˺”*), the affair conducted from heaven to earth and ascending back on a day of reckoning (32:5 — *“He conducts every affair from the heavens to the earth, then it all ascends to Him on a Day whose length is a thousand years by your counting”*). Verse 34 puts the same doctrine into a physical object. The stone falling on a specific roof was specified before it fell, which means the register existed before the crime reached its limit. The chapter's fourth oath described the angels as apportioning affairs by command (51:4 — *“and ˹the angels˺ administering affairs by ˹Allah’s˺ command”*); this verse shows the apportionment in its most severe application.

**The Same Precision Appears in the Chapter's Other Cases**

The four destructions narrated in this chapter are all described with the same attention to the instrument and its exactness. ʿĀd receives a wind that leaves nothing it passes over unruined (51:41–42 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ ’Âd ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent against them the devastating wind There was nothing it came upon that it did not reduce to ashes”*). Thamūd receives a single blast while they look on (51:44 — *“Still they persisted in defying the commands of their Lord, so they were overtaken by a ˹mighty˺ blast while they were looking on”*). Pharaoh and his soldiers are seized and thrown into the sea (51:40 — *“So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea while he was blameworthy”*). In each case the punishment fits the crime, uses the element the people trusted, and arrives at a stated time. Verse 34 is the clearest statement of the principle behind all four: the punishment is designated, not general. That is what allows the chapter to present destruction as evidence of order rather than as evidence of chaos.
verses.35:
> Then ˹before the torment˺ We evacuated the believers from the city

**The Timing Is Given to the Hour**

Another account fixes the moment: *“We unleashed upon them a storm of stones. As for ˹the believers of˺ Lot’s family, We delivered them before dawn”* (54:34). Before dawn — the same hour this chapter elsewhere names as the time when the devout seek forgiveness (51:18 — *“and pray for forgiveness before dawn”*). The coincidence of hours is not accidental in Qur'anic narrative; the last part of the night is repeatedly the time of deliverance and of response. The instruction given to the household matches it: *“So travel with your family in the dark of night, and do not let any of you look back, except your wife.”* (11:81). The departure, the journey, and the arrival are all placed inside a single night, and the morning is named as the appointed time of the city.

**Do Not Look Back**

The condition attached to the evacuation is a prohibition on turning around. The instruction is practical and symbolic at once. Practically, a family fleeing at night through a doomed region gains nothing by looking and loses time by stopping. Symbolically, the look back is attachment to the place being destroyed, and the one person exempted from the command is the one already marked for the same fate: except your wife. The Qur'an does not explain her attachment, and the commentators differ about its nature, but the narrative treats her exclusion as settled in advance. She will suffer the fate of the others (11:81 — *“She will certainly suffer the fate of the others.”*), and the determination is described as already made (15:60 — *“except his wife. We have determined that she will be one of the doomed.””*).

**Punishment Waits for the Believers to Leave**

The principle is stated elsewhere in general terms: *“But Allah would never punish them while you ˹O Prophet˺ were in their midst. Nor would He ever punish them if they prayed for forgiveness.”* (8:33). The presence of a righteous person in a community delays its destruction. In the case of Lot's city the delay runs to its logical end: the righteous are removed first, and only then does the punishment fall. The same sequence appears in the account of ʿĀd, where the believers are saved and the disbelievers uprooted (7:72 — *“So We saved him and those with him by Our mercy and uprooted those who denied Our signs. They were not believers”*). What the pattern establishes is that divine punishment is never a disaster that sweeps up the innocent along with the guilty. The innocent are relocated before it begins.

**Here They Are Called Believers, and Next Submitters**

Verse 35 uses *muʾminūn*, believers; verse 36 uses *muslimūn*, those who have submitted. The commentators read the pairing as describing people who combine faith with action, and the two terms are used elsewhere in the Qur'an with a deliberate distinction between inward conviction and outward compliance (49:14 — *“But say, ‘We have submitted,’ for faith has not yet entered your hearts.”*). In this passage the sequence moves from the inward designation to the outward one, which fits the narrative: what is being described is a household that left a city at night on an instruction, an act of submission performed on the basis of belief. Both words are needed to describe them completely, and both are supplied in consecutive verses.

**The Verse Sets Up the Count**

Verse 35 says the believers were brought out; verse 36 says how many there were. The two verses together produce the chapter's starkest statistic: one house. The narration does not comment on the number or moralise about it. It states the extraction and then the count, and leaves the reader to absorb what a city containing one believing household deserves. The following verse then describes what was left behind as a sign, which completes the sequence — removal, destruction, and a remaining trace for those who fear the painful punishment (51:37 — *“And We have left a sign there ˹as a lesson˺ for those who fear the painful punishment”*).

> But We only found one family that had submitted ˹to Allah˺

**One House: Lot and His Two Daughters**

The commentators identify the household as Lot together with his two daughters, saved from the punishment while his wife was not. The identification is consistent across the parallel accounts: *“So We saved him and his family except his wife, who was one of the doomed.”* (7:83), *“So We saved him and all of his family, except an old woman, who was one of the doomed.”* (26:170–171). *“So We delivered him and his family, except his wife. We had destined her to be one of the doomed.”* (27:57). Three separate chapters give the same arithmetic: a household rescued minus one member. The verse in front of us states the result of that arithmetic in the smallest possible unit — one house.

**The Wife Is Excluded From the House That Was Saved**

Her exclusion is stated as a determination rather than an accident. In al-Ḥijr the angels say: *“As for the family of Lot, we will certainly deliver them all, except his wife. We have determined that she will be one of the doomed.”* (15:59–60). The exception is made inside a promise of total deliverance, which is the sharpest form the statement could take. Kinship with a prophet does not transfer salvation. The same principle is enacted in the accounts of Noah's son and in the description of the day when no soul benefits another (82:19 — *“˹It is˺ the Day no soul will be of ˹any˺ benefit to another whatsoever, for all authority on that Day belongs to Allah ˹entirely˺”*). Verse 36 depends on this: the household counted as one house of submitters does not include every relative of its head.

**Submission After Belief**

Verse 35 described those brought out as believers; this verse describes what was found as a house of those who submitted. The two terms are used with care elsewhere in the Qur'an. When some nomadic Arabs claim belief, they are told: *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ ‘You have not believed. But say, ‘We have submitted,’ for faith has not yet entered your hearts.’”* (49:14). Submission can exist without full faith, and faith without visible submission is not the Qur'an's concern. Here the order is reversed and complementary: the people are first named for their belief and then for the act that belief produced — leaving a city at night because they were told to. The commentators read the pairing as describing those who join faith to action.

**A Majority Is Not Evidence of Anything**

The Qur'an states this rule in flat terms and repeats it: *“And most people will not believe—no matter how keen you are—”* (12:103), and *“˹O Prophet!˺ If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way.”* (6:116). Verse 36 is the narrative form of the same claim. A city's size, wealth, and unanimity carry no weight in the finding. The chapter's audience lived in a commercial centre that prided itself on its consensus and its ancestral practice, and the story places that pride against a count of one household. The comparison is not flattering to the majority, and it is not intended to be.

**What Remains After the Count**

Two verses have now described the removal and the finding. The next verse describes what was left in the place afterwards: a sign for those who fear the painful punishment (51:37 — *“And We have left a sign there ˹as a lesson˺ for those who fear the painful punishment”*). The sequence is complete — inspection, extraction, destruction, residue — and each stage is stated in a single verse. One case has been established with enough detail to serve as a precedent, and three more will follow in shorter form.
verses.37:
> And We have left a sign there ˹as a lesson˺ for those who fear the painful punishment

**The Ruins Lie on a Route People Still Use**

The Qur'an insists on the accessibility of the remains. *“Their ruins still lie along a known route. Surely in this is a sign for those who believe.”* (15:76–77). The road is specified as known, which means travelled, and the audience is the one using it. Another chapter puts it even more directly to the Meccans: *“You ˹Meccans˺ certainly pass by their ruins day and night. Will you not then understand?”* (37:137–138). Passing by twice daily and not understanding is the exact failure the verse in front of us addresses. The sign is not hidden in a desert that requires an expedition; it sits beside a commercial route used by the very people disputing the chapter's opening oaths.

**Ruined Houses Make the Argument Without Words**

Another chapter describes the same kind of remains in the same terms: *“So their homes are there, ˹but completely˺ ruined because of their wrongdoing. Surely in this is a lesson for people of knowledge.”* (27:52). The causal clause is the point — because of their wrongdoing. The ruin is not presented as a natural decay but as a consequence with a reason attached, and the reason is legible from the site.

**Meccan Caravans Passed Within Sight**

The audience's relation to these ruins is economic as well as geographic. The trade routes that carried Meccan caravans north passed the region of the destroyed cities. The Qur'an elsewhere ties the people of ʿĀd and Thamūd to visible remains the Meccans could inspect themselves: *“And the people of ’Ȃd and Thamûd ˹met a similar fate˺, which must be clear to you ˹Meccans˺ from their ruins.”* (29:38). The clarity is stated as something already available, not as a claim requiring acceptance. Verse 37 places Lot's city in the same category of public evidence. The sign is left in the open, on a road, in a region the audience visits, which removes the usual excuse of inaccessible proof.

**Fear Is the Capacity That Reads a Sign**

The chapter has now named two capacities required for its evidence: certainty (51:20 — *“There are ˹countless˺ signs on earth for those with sure faith”*) and fear (51:37 — *“And We have left a sign there ˹as a lesson˺ for those who fear the painful punishment”*). Neither is an intellectual skill. Both are dispositions that determine what a person does with what he sees. Certainty allows signs in the earth and in the self to function as proofs; fear allows a ruin to function as a warning. A person lacking the second will look at the same stones and conclude that civilizations fall. That conclusion is true and useless. The verse specifies the audience because it knows the material will be misread by everyone else, and because the misreading is not an intellectual error but a failure of seriousness about consequences.

**The Narrative Block Now Shortens**

Twelve verses have been given to Abraham's household and the destruction that followed it. The three cases that come next are compressed: Moses in three verses (51:38–40 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ Moses ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent him to Pharaoh with compelling proof but Pharaoh was carried away by his power, saying ˹of Moses˺, “A magician or a madman!” So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea while he was blameworthy”*), ʿĀd in two (51:41–42 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ ’Âd ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent against them the devastating wind There was nothing it came upon that it did not reduce to ashes”*), Thamūd in three (51:43–45 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ Thamûd ˹was another lesson,˺ when they were told, “Enjoy yourselves ˹only˺ for a ˹short˺ while.” Still they persisted in defying the commands of their Lord, so they were overtaken by a ˹mighty˺ blast while they were looking on Then they were not able to rise up, nor were they helped”*), and Noah in one (51:46 — *“And the people of Noah ˹had also been destroyed˺ earlier. They were truly a rebellious people”*). The chapter has established its method in detail and now runs it at speed. Each case will follow the same shape — a messenger sent, a warning refused, a punishment executed by a specific instrument — and the reader is expected to supply the rest from the first telling. Verse 37 closes the long version of the pattern; what follows are its summaries.
verses.38:
> And in ˹the story of˺ Moses ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent him to Pharaoh with compelling proof

**Words Are Deliberately Left Out**

The Arabic reads simply "and in Moses" — a phrase with no verb and no predicate. The translation supplies what the pattern of the chapter requires: was another lesson, or was a sign. The same elliptical construction governs the three cases that follow: and in ʿĀd (51:41 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ ’Âd ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent against them the devastating wind”*), and in Thamūd (51:43 — *“And in ˹the story of˺ Thamûd ˹was another lesson,˺ when they were told, “Enjoy yourselves ˹only˺ for a ˹short˺ while.””*), and the people of Noah earlier (51:46 — *“And the people of Noah ˹had also been destroyed˺ earlier. They were truly a rebellious people”*). Once the first instance is established, the rest are listed by name alone, and the reader completes each one from the shared structure. The device is economical and it makes a point: these are not four separate stories but four specimens of one thing. Naming them without verbs treats them as items in a series already understood.

**The Proof Is Delivered Before Anything Else Happens**

The verse's order is the argument's order: sent, then given proof, then rejected, then seized. Nothing about the punishment appears before the evidence has been presented. The same sequence is stated as a rule elsewhere: *“And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺.”* (17:15). In the account of Moses the proof is described in concrete terms — the great sign shown to Pharaoh (79:20 — *“Then Moses showed him the great sign”*) — and Moses' own message states its character: *“And do not be arrogant with Allah. I have certainly come to you with a compelling proof.”* (44:19). The identical phrase appears in both chapters, which fixes its technical sense: a warrant enough to oblige the hearer.

**Moses Is the Most Frequently Named Prophet in the Book**

His name appears 136 times in the Qur'an, more than any other prophet — Abraham is named 69 times, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is named four times, though addressed constantly. The count is not trivia. It explains why the Qur'an can compress Moses' story to three verses here and still expect the audience to follow: they already know the case in detail from longer accounts in 20:9–97 — *“Has the story of Moses reached you ˹O Prophet˺”*, 26:10–66 — *“˹Remember˺ when your Lord called out to Moses, “Go to the wrongdoing people”*, 28:3–46 — *“We narrate to you ˹O Prophet˺ part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe”*, and 7:103–155 — *“Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wrongfully rejected them. See what was the end of the corruptors”*. Adh-Dhāriyāt is quoting a story its hearers have heard many times, and selecting from it only the elements the chapter's argument needs — the proof, the refusal, the seizure. Compression of this kind is possible only where the material is already common property.

**In a Meccan Chapter the Story Is an Argument, Not a History**

The commentators note that in the Meccan sūrahs which feature Moses — here, in 40:23–45 — *“Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs and compelling proof”*, 43:46–56 — *“Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said: “I am a messenger of the Lord of all worlds.””*, 44:17–31 — *“Indeed, before them We tested Pharaoh’s people: a noble messenger came to them”*, and 79:15–25 — *“Has the story of Moses reached you ˹O Prophet˺”* — the account functions as a spiritual example reflecting aspects of the Prophet Muhammad's own challenge rather than as narrative history. The point is confirmed by the chapter's placement. Moses faces a ruler who cannot answer his proofs and so insults him instead; the Prophet ﷺ faces a commercial elite that cannot answer his recitation and so calls him a magician or a madman (51:52 — *“Similarly, no messenger came to those before them without being told: “A magician or a madman!””*). The parallel is not incidental. It is the reason this story is told here, in this order, in this length.

**Pharaoh's Position Is Stated Before His Response**

The transgression is named in the sending itself. He has exceeded all bounds (20:43 — *“Go, both of you, to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺”*; 79:17 — *“˹commanding,˺ “Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺”*), and elsewhere he is called a tyrant and a transgressor (44:31 — *“of Pharaoh. He was truly a tyrant, a transgressor”*). The chapter gives the reader the diagnosis before the quotation of his words, so that his response can be evaluated rather than merely recorded. This is a deliberate arrangement. A reader who hears "a magician or a madman" without knowing the speaker's condition might treat it as an argument; hearing it after being told that the speaker has transgressed all bounds and has been shown a clear warrant identifies it correctly as evasion. Verse 38 does that preparatory work in a single clause.

Two men are sent to a tyrant, and they are told: *“Go, both of you, to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺. Speak to him gently, so perhaps he may be mindful ˹of Me˺ or fearful ˹of My punishment˺.”* (20:43–44).

> but Pharaoh was carried away by his power, saying ˹of Moses˺, “A magician or a madman!”

**Tawallā: He Turned His Back**

The verb describes turning away, withdrawing, giving one's back. Another chapter narrates the same movement and adds what followed it: *“Then Moses showed him the great sign, but he denied and disobeyed ˹Allah˺, then turned his back, striving ˹against the truth˺.”* (79:20–22). Three acts in sequence — denial, disobedience, turning — and then active effort against the truth. Verse 39 compresses the whole movement into one word and attaches the support he turned with.

**Two Accusations That Cannot Both Be True**

A magician has skill, training, technique, and intention; a madman has none of these. The two descriptions exclude each other, and the verse offers them joined by "or," which is the mark of a person selecting from available insults rather than stating a finding. This is precisely the condition the chapter diagnosed at its start: *“Surely you are ˹lost˺ in conflicting views ˹regarding the truth˺.”* (51:8). Pharaoh's response is the same contradiction in a single mouth. The Qur'an notes the repetition of the charge across history in the verse that generalises it: *“Similarly, no messenger came to those before them without being told: ‘A magician or a madman!’”* (51:52). The pairing is a formula, and a formula is not an argument.

**The Same Charge Is Recorded Against Moses Everywhere**

The accusation appears at every stage of the confrontation. The chiefs of Pharaoh's people say it first: *“He is indeed a skilled magician”* (7:109). Pharaoh repeats it to his court: *“He is indeed a skilled magician”* (26:34). It is used of the message itself in another encounter: *“But they responded: ‘Magician! Total liar!’”* (40:24). The consistency across accounts shows that the charge was the standard response of an established authority to a messenger it could not refute. The Quraysh used the same vocabulary of the Prophet ﷺ — magician, poet, madman, a man taught by another — and the chapter treats the repetition as evidence about the speakers rather than about the messengers.

**His Boast Is Recorded Elsewhere in the Same Terms**

The content of Pharaoh's confidence is given in another chapter, where he addresses his people from a position of strength: *“O my people! Am I not sovereign over Egypt as well as ˹all˺ these streams flowing at my feet? Can you not see? Am I not better than this nobody who can hardly express himself?”* (43:51–52). Kingdom, rivers, eloquence, and social standing are set against a man with no army and a speech impediment. That is the *rukn* of verse 39 itemised.

**The Claim of Lordship Follows the Same Movement**

The turning described here ends in an explicit claim. Another account narrates the escalation: he summoned his people and called out, *"I am your lord, the most high!"* and God overtook him, making him an example in this life and the next (79:23–25 — *“Then he summoned ˹his people˺ and called out”*). The path runs from a proof shown, to a denial, to a turning away with one's support, to a public claim of divinity, to seizure. Verse 39 sits at the third stage, and it is the stage at which the outcome is effectively decided. A man who has turned his back on a clear warrant while leaning on his army has no further move available except to enlarge himself, and enlargement is what the next stage records.
verses.40:
> So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea while he was blameworthy

**One Verb Covers the Whole Event**

The verb is *akhadhnā*, we seized — a single act with no battle, no campaign, no sequence of engagements. The Qur'an's accounts of the drowning preserve this compression: *“So We inspired Moses: ‘Strike the sea with your staff,’ and the sea was split, each part was like a huge mountain. We drew the pursuers to that place, and delivered Moses and those with him all together. Then We drowned the others.”* (26:63–66). Verse 40 states the same thing in even shorter form.

**Mulīm: A Man Who Has Earned Blame**

The closing description is *mulīm*, one who is blameworthy, deserving of reproach. The word is used elsewhere in a strikingly different case: *“Then the whale engulfed him while he was blameworthy.”* (37:142), of Jonah in the belly of the fish. The shared term connects two men who both went into water under blame and were treated differently, and it fixes the sense of the word here. Pharaoh's blame is stated as a condition he has brought on himself, not as a charge laid against him by an opponent. He transgressed all bounds (79:17 — *“˹commanding,˺ “Go to Pharaoh, for he has truly transgressed ˹all bounds˺”*), turned away relying on his power (51:39 — *“but Pharaoh was carried away by his power, saying ˹of Moses˺, “A magician or a madman!””*), and claimed lordship (79:24 — *“saying, “I am your lord, the most high!””*). The drowning is described with the blame already attached, as its explanation.

**The Corpse Was Preserved as an Exhibit**

The event did not end with the drowning. *“Today We will preserve your corpse so that you may become an example for those who come after you. And surely most people are heedless of Our examples!”* (10:92). The preservation is stated as an act with a purpose, and the purpose is the same one described in verse 37 for the ruins of Lot's city: a sign left for later people. The closing complaint — most people are heedless of Our examples — connects this verse to the heedlessness of 51:11 — *“those who are ˹steeped˺ in ignorance, totally heedless”*. Two exhibits are described in this chapter's narrative block, one a ruined city on a road and one a body kept from decay, and both address the same failure to look.

**He Was Made an Example in Two Worlds**

Another chapter states the scope of the outcome: *“So Allah overtook him, making him an example in this life and the next. Surely in this is a lesson for whoever stands in awe of ˹Allah˺.”* (79:25–26). The exemplary function is not limited to the historical event. Pharaoh becomes a permanent reference point for the chapter's audience and for every later one, and the audience is again specified — whoever stands in awe. The qualification matches verse 37's "those who fear the painful punishment." Both verses attach their evidence to a disposition, which is the chapter's consistent method: the material is public, the benefit is conditional.

**The Seizure Is a General Law, Not a Special Case**

The Qur'an generalises the event in a verse that reads as a rule: *“Such is the ˹crushing˺ grip of your Lord when He seizes the societies entrenched in wrongdoing. Indeed, His grip is ˹terribly˺ painful and severe.”* (11:102). Pharaoh's case is presented as an instance of a standing practice, and the practice is described with the same verb used in verse 40. This is what makes the narrative block useful to the chapter's argument. The mockers of verse 12 asked when the day would come; the four cases that follow show a grip that has been applied repeatedly, to societies that believed themselves permanent.

The same event is narrated elsewhere with the sea closing over the pursuers: *“And leave the sea parted, for they are certainly an army bound to drown.”* (44:24).

Pharaoh's army followed the Israelites onto a divided seabed, and the same water closed on the pursuers: *“And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes.”* (2:50).

The Qur'an records Pharaoh's final words and their rejection: *“But as Pharaoh was drowning, he cried out, ‘I believe that there is no god except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am ˹now˺ one of those who submit.’ ˹He was told,˺ ‘Now ˹you believe˺? But you always disobeyed and were one of the corruptors.’”* (10:90–91).
verses.41:
> And in ˹the story of˺ ’Âd ˹was another lesson,˺ when We sent against them the devastating wind

**ʿĀd Were an Arabian Tribe of Builders**

The people in question were a pre-Islamic Arabian tribe, not a distant nation, and the Qur'an describes them with admiration for their physical achievement: *“Did you not see how your Lord dealt with ’Ȃd— ˹the people˺ of Iram—with ˹their˺ great stature, unmatched in any other land”* (89:6–8). Their own boast is recorded: *“As for ’Ȃd, they acted arrogantly throughout the land with no right, boasting, ‘Who is superior to us in might?’”* (41:15). The verse that follows supplies the answer to the boast — did they not see that the One who created them was far superior in might. Strength, architecture, and stature are the specific qualities the case turns on, and the wind that destroys them is an opponent none of those qualities can resist.

**Rīḥ ʿAqīm Is a Wind That Gives Nothing**

The adjective is *ʿaqīm*, barren. The commentators explain it precisely: a wind carrying no rain and pollinating no trees, unlike the winds this chapter swore by at its opening (51:1 — *“By the winds scattering ˹dust˺”*). The same word described Sarah's condition nine verses earlier (51:29 — *“Then his wife came forward with a cry, clasping her forehead ˹in astonishment˺, exclaiming, “˹A baby from˺ a barren, old woman!””*), where it meant a womb that produces nothing. Applied to weather, it names a force stripped of every benefit winds normally bring — no fertilising, no driving of clouds, no filling of sails.

**Elsewhere the Wind Is Described as Furious and Howling**

The Qur'an gives this wind several descriptions, and they accumulate. It is a furious wind sent for several miserable days to make them taste a humiliating punishment in this life (41:16 — *“So We sent against them a furious wind, for ˹several˺ miserable days, to make them taste a humiliating punishment in this worldly life.”*); a furious wind on a day of unrelenting misery (54:19 — *“Indeed, We sent against them a furious wind, on a day of unrelenting misery”*); and, most emphatically, a furious, bitter wind unleashed on them non-stop (69:6–7 — *“And as for ’Ȃd, they were destroyed by a furious, bitter wind”*). The addition of duration matters: seven nights and eight days. The wind is not a gust or a storm but a sustained operation with a beginning and an end, which fits the chapter's theme of decrees executed on schedule. What began as a boast about might ends as a counting of days.

**Hūd Was Their Messenger**

The warning came from one of their own: *“And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, ‘O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him. You do nothing but fabricate lies ˹against Allah˺.’”* (11:50). The charge is the same one every messenger in this chapter brings, and the accusation of fabrication is answered by the destruction described in verse 41. The Qur'an summarises the outcome in a single verse that reads like a verdict: *“That was ’Âd.
